extracted.intended_audience: general readers of The Spectator; men and women seeking advice on conduct, education, and domestic relations
extracted.subtask_description: An early-18th-century moral/conduct essay offering evaluative standards and practical rules about education, public behaviour, good-nature, and the management of jealousy in marriage. It mixes description of faults with prescriptive remedies and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher behaviour: polite in behaviour and method of teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: We had a Set of Men, polite in their Behaviour and Method of Teaching, who should be put into a Condition of being above flattering or fearing the Parents of those they instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If instructors are independent of parental influence and behave politely, 'we might then possibly see Learning become a Pleasure, and Children delighting themselves in that which now they abhor.' Such instructors should not flatter or fear parents; their freedom would prevent pedantry and ensure only those with genius are bred to learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harshness as a pedagogical method
rubrics_metrics.description: He never gives any of us an harsh Word, and we think it the greatest Punishment in the World when he will not speak to any of us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gentle, affectionate treatment (absence of harsh words) makes learning pleasurable and motivates children; withholding attention is an effective chastisement compared to harsh verbal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not breed pedants; only educate those with genius
rubrics_metrics.description: We should have no more Pedants, nor any bred to Learning who had not Genius for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper independent instructors would prevent the production of mere pedants—education should cultivate innate genius rather than force learning on those unsuited for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and discourage 'sets' of impertinents in public assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: A Party who came thither together, or whose Impertinencies are of an equal Pitch, act in Concert ... sometimes a Set of Whisperers ... sometimes a Set of Laughers ... whose whole Business is to draw off the Attention of the Spectators from the Entertainment, and to fix it upon themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize types (whisperers, laughers) who disturb public entertainments (opera, play, water-works). These sets disrespect the company and degrade the occasion; public decency requires their suppression or correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impertinence often arises from social mimicry (footmen influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: I am at a loss to know from whom People of Fortune should learn this Behaviour, unless it be from the Footmen who keep their Places at a new Play ... passing away their Time in Sets at All-fours ... with a perfect Disregard to People of Quality sitting on each Side of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-born persons may imitate vulgar or inattentive manners seen among servants; recognising sources of bad behaviour can inform corrective measures and social instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalize those who disturb public assemblies (suggested policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For preserving therefore the Decency of publick Assemblies, methinks it would be but reasonable that those who Disturb others should pay at least a double Price for their Places; or rather Women of Birth and Distinction should be informed that a Levity of Behaviour ... degrades them below their meanest Attendants; and Gentlemen should know that a fine Coat is a Livery, when the Person who wears it discovers no higher Sense than that of a Footman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination of financial penalty, social admonition to women of rank, and reminding gentlemen that outward dress is worthless without higher conduct is proposed as remedies to restore decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature preferred to wit in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-nature is more agreeable in Conversation than Wit, and gives a certain Air to the Countenance which is more amiable than Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-nature makes virtue appear fairer, mitigates vice, and makes folly and impertinence supportable. In social estimation, affability and gentleness often outshine mere cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-breeding is imitation of good-nature; beware mere artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-Breeding ... is nothing else but an Imitation and Mimickry of Good-nature ... These exterior Shows and Appearances of Humanity render a Man wonderfully popular and beloved when they are founded upon a real Good-nature; but without it are like Hypocrisy ... which, when it is discovered, makes a Man more detestable than professed Impiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polished manners are valuable only insofar as they reflect genuine benevolence; mere formal politeness without real feeling becomes hypocrisy and is more offensive than open vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature is native and improvable but not producible by education
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-nature is generally born with us: ... Education may improve but not produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While upbringing and circumstances (health, prosperity, kind treatment) nourish good-nature, it is primarily a natural disposition that cannot be wholly manufactured by schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercy and pardon as part of good-nature — limited by justice
rubrics_metrics.description: This Part of Good-nature, however, which consists in the pardoning and overlooking of Faults, is to be exercised only in doing our selves Justice, and that too in the ordinary Commerce and Occurrences of Life; for in the publick Administrations of Justice, Mercy to one may be Cruelty to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private leniency and overlooking faults is virtuous in daily life, but in public or legal contexts such mercy may harm others and therefore should be constrained by justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-nature often mistaken for wit; good-natured writers may be underrated
rubrics_metrics.description: It is grown almost into a Maxim, that Good-natured Men are not always Men of the most Wit. This Observation ... has no Foundation in Nature. ... Ill-nature among ordinary Observers passes for Wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire or spite often elicits quick public laughter and can be mistaken for cleverness; writers of good-natured humour may find less reception in print though they shine in private company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of jealousy as a passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is that Pain which a Man feels from the Apprehension that he is not equally beloved by the Person whom he entirely loves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jealousy is characterized by doubtfulness and an appetite for discovery that often finds nothing; its pleasure arises perversely from disappointment and pursuit of imagined secrets, making it difficult to cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy's effects: alienation of the beloved and self-fulfilling guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy naturally tends to alienate the Affection which it is so solicitous to engross ... it often draws after it a more fatal Train of Consequences, and makes the Person you suspect guilty of the very Crimes you are so much afraid of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive suspicion constrains behaviour and shows low opinion, prompting the suspected person toward resentment or actual infidelity; jealousy thus destroys its own object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of men most susceptible to jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: The First ... conscious to themselves of an Infirmity ... A Second Sort ... cunning, wary, and distrustful Tempers ... Now what these Men fancy they know of Women by Reflection, your lewd and vicious Men believe they have learned by Experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Insecure men (weakness, age, deformity), 2) over-refining/distrustful men (who construct plots), 3) men hardened by vice (who project their own unfaithfulness) are most prone to jealousy; understanding the type informs how to address it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical/temperamental observation about jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is no Northern Passion, but rages most in those Nations that lie nearest the Influence of the Sun ... Our own Nation is very temperately situated in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay attributes variations in jealousy to temperament/climate, using this as a general observation rather than a prescriptive rule—useful for contextualising prevalence of the passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for wives: never admire in another what the jealous man lacks
rubrics_metrics.description: You never seem to dislike in another what the Jealous Man is himself guilty of, or to admire any thing in which he himself does not excel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not praise or openly admire qualities in others that the husband lacks, since commendation of such qualities will inflame jealousy; tailor visible admiration to what he possesses or values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for wives: be free, open, and transparent in conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: You must be sure to be free and open in your Conversation with him, and to let in Light upon your Actions, to unravel all your Designs, and discover every Secret however trifling or indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid winks, whispers, secrecy; make the jealous husband a principal confidant and maintain uniform sincerity—opacity breeds suspicion and the imagination will invent plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional remedy: show genuine distress when falsely suspected
rubrics_metrics.description: If both these Methods fail, the best way will be to let him see you are much cast down and afflicted for the ill Opinion he entertains of you ... a melancholy, dejected Carriage ... may soften the jealous Husband into Pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated sorrow and wounded innocence may awaken pity and reduce jealous suspicions; beware that affected coldness or teasing can harden contempt and destroy affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeited jealousy as a dangerous artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: This is to change Sides for a while with the jealous Man, and to turn his own Passion upon himself; to take some Occasion of growing Jealous of him ... This Counterfeited Jealousy ... is an Artifice so difficult, and at the same time so dis-ingenuous, that it ought never to be put in Practice, but by such as have Skill enough to cover the Deceit, and Innocence to render it excusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feigning jealousy can placate or punish a jealous spouse but is morally dubious and risky—only the extremely skilled and morally secure should consider it, and even then cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical/cautionary exempla (Herod and Mariamne)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Story of Herod and Mariamne ... may serve almost as an Example to whatever can be said on this Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative historical examples demonstrate how jealousy can escalate to tragedy; such exempla serve as moral warnings and rhetorical reinforcement of the preceding rules.
